t:
Among the given halides, which one will give the same constitutional isomer product in both S_N1 and S_N2 reactions? (I)
[[img:f976e012afce]]
[[img:dae6b6ddde26]]
[[img:8a9e5f62d4ce]]
[[img:8d5c4a080ae9]]
s:
In an S_N2 reaction, the nucleophile attacks the carbon bearing the leaving group, giving a product with the same carbon skeleton connectivity as the reactant.
In an S_N1 reaction, a carbocation intermediate is formed. If this carbocation undergoes a rearrangement (such as a hydride or alkyl shift) to form a more stable carbocation, the nucleophile will attack the new position, leading to a product with a different constitution. If no rearrangement occurs, the S_N1 and S_N2 pathways will yield the same constitutional isomer.
For halide (I), the S_N2 reaction produces substitution at C2. In the S_N1 pathway, heterolysis forms a secondary carbocation at C2 with 5 α-hydrogens. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 would generate a secondary carbocation at C3 with only 3 α-hydrogens, which is less stable. Thus, no rearrangement occurs, and the S_N1 product is also substituted at C2. The constitutional isomers are the same.
For halide (II), the S_N2 reaction gives substitution at C1. In the S_N1 pathway, the initial secondary carbocation at C1 undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift from C2 to form a more stable tertiary carbocation. Nucleophilic attack at C2 yields a structurally different product. The constitutional isomers are different.
For halide (III), the initial intermediate is a secondary cyclohexyl carbocation. Any hydride shift would merely form an identical secondary carbocation. Since there is no net rearrangement, both S_N1 and S_N2 reactions yield the same constitutional isomer.
For halide (IV), the intermediate is a secondary sec-butyl carbocation. A 1,2-hydride shift would form another equivalent secondary carbocation, offering no stability advantage. Thus, no rearrangement occurs, and both mechanisms yield a product substituted at C2. The constitutional isomers are the same.
Therefore, halides (I), (III), and (IV) will give the same constitutional isomer in both S_N1 and S_N2 reactions. .

t: On on heating diethyl ether with conc- HI, 2 moles of which of the following is formed
s:
Firstly the HI given will get ionized:
Hl→H⁺+I⁻
The iodide ion produced will attack one of the Carbon-oxygen bonds, gets attached to carbon, the hydrogen ion produced in the first step will get attached to a negatively charged oxygen atom:
CH₃CH₂O−CH₂CH₃+HI→CH₃CH₂OH+I−CH₂−CH₃
The ethanol produced in the above step still has a carbon-oxygen bond and we are provided with an excess of HI (concentrated), so the iodide ion will now attack the carbon-oxygen bond of ethanol similarly, and the hydrogen ion will get attached to hydroxide ion produced:
CH₃CH₂−OH+HI→CH₃CH₂−I+H₂O
Thus, the overall reaction between diethyl ether and hot and concentrated HI will be:
CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃+2Hl→2CH₃CH₂I+H₂O
Means, the given reaction will give two moles of ethyl iodide. .

t: Which of the following statement is correct for the reactivity in S_N2 reaction?
s: The electronegativity order of hybridized carbons is sp>sp²>sp³ . So in an allylic halide, such as CH₂=CH−CH₂−I , the alpha carbon is much more partially positive than the alpha carbon in CH₃−CH₂−CH₂I . Therefore, the attacking nucleophile will be attracted to the alpha carbon more in the allylic halide compound than in the primary halide. Hence, allylic halides tend to follow S_N2 pathways more than primary halides.
